transcript.text:
I'm sorry to hear your fridge isn't cooling. This is a common issue, and it usually comes down to one of two things: either the cold air isn't reaching the fridge compartment (often because a fan has failed or ice is blocking the airflow), or the cooling system itself isn't working. To narrow this down quickly, I need to know what's happening in the freezer section:
1. Is the freezer still freezing properly (e.g. are your frozen foods hard)?
2. Inside the freezer, look at the back wall. Is there a thick layer of ice or frost on it? Please let me know these two things, and we'll take it from there.
freezer still freezing, ice cream hard. yes thick frost on back wall, more than ive ever seen

That pattern—a still-cold freezer but a warm fridge, combined with thick frost on the back wall—is a common sign of a defrost system failure. Here is what is happening: Your fridge-freezer has one cooling coil hidden behind that frosted panel in the freezer. A fan pushes cold air from there into the fridge section. The appliance runs an automatic defrost cycle to melt ice off that coil, but if a part (usually the heater or the thermostat/sensor) fails, the ice never melts. It builds up into a solid block of snow/ice that chokes the airflow. The fan might still be spinning, but it can't push cold air through the ice block, so the freezer stays cold (because the coil is right there) but the fridge goes warm. To confirm this and get you cooling again temporarily, we need to do a full manual defrost:
1. Switch the appliance off at the wall socket.
2. Remove all food (use cool bags/ice packs if possible).
3. Leave both doors open until every bit of ice in the freezer has melted completely. You may want towels down for water.
4. Dry it out, plug it back in, and set it to normal. Does the fridge start cooling properly again after this full defrost? (Note: If it does, it suggests a part needs replacing, as the ice will build up again within a few days.)
ok will try that, got a cool box for the food. no burning smell or tripping btw. back tomorrow

That sounds like the right plan. The combination of a still-cold freezer but a warm fridge, along with that heavy frost build-up on the back wall, points to a failure in the automatic defrost system. Here is what is likely happening: Your fridge-freezer has one cooling coil hidden behind that frosted panel. A fan pushes cold air from there into the fridge section. If a part (usually the heater or the thermostat/sensor) fails, the ice never melts. It builds up into a solid block of snow/ice that chokes the airflow. The fan might still be spinning, but it can't push cold air through the ice block, so the freezer stays cold (because the coil is right there) but the fridge goes warm. The manual defrost you are about to do will clear this blockage temporarily and should restore cooling. However, if a part has failed, the ice will build up again within a few days until that specific component is replaced. 1. Does the fridge start cooling properly again after you've done the full defrost?
2. If it does, do you notice the thick frost building up again within 3–5 days? This will confirm whether we are dealing with a simple blockage or a part that needs replacing.
did the defrost, fridge was back to 3C within a day. now about 5 days on and it's starting to creep up again

That suggests it: the fridge cools fine after you clear the ice, but the ice builds back up within a few days. 1. The defrost heater (which melts the ice) has burned out and won't heat up.
2. The defrost thermostat/sensor (which tells the heater when to turn on) has failed open and is never calling for a defrost cycle. To tell them apart, we need to look at the components inside the freezer. Please unplug the fridge, remove all shelves in the freezer, and take off the rear plastic panel (usually held by screws or clips). Behind it you will see the evaporator coils. 1. Is there a solid block of ice packed over those coils?
2. Do you see a metal heating element (strip or coil) and a small thermostat (cylinder with wires)? If so, are they intact, or is there any visible damage, melting, or burn marks on them? Once you check that, I can tell you exactly which part to replace.
cant take the back panel off, no idea how and dont want to break the clips. no multimeter either. anything else I can check?

Since you can't open the panel and don't have a multimeter to test the heating element or thermostat directly, we have to rely on what we've already seen. The fact that the fridge cools perfectly after a manual defrost but ices up again within five days suggests the automatic defrost cycle is not happening. Both are common failures and both require replacing the part behind that back panel. Because this involves accessing internal components and testing electrical parts, I recommend calling a qualified appliance engineer to replace the faulty defrost component (usually the heater or the bi-metal thermostat). It is not a sealed system issue like gas or refrigerant leak, so it should be a straightforward repair for them. Trying to force the panel off without knowing how your specific model is clipped together risks breaking the liner, which would cause a refrigerant leak and make the fridge unrepairable.
